utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my country, to consult an expert before the trial begins is not permissible. The expert is consulted in front of the Trial Chamber that called for the expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, let me pose a situation to you which may not arise in practice in your jurisdiction, but if it does I would be interested in the answer. Certainly in an adversarial system, it is often the case that when someone is killed, a post mortem is carried out at the time, and then the body is cremated or, indeed, buried but at least when cremated there is absolutely no possibility of access to the body. Subsequently, there is a trial of a person who's discovered to be the culprit, and he wants his own pathologist to advise him as an expert. Are you saying that before the trial that pathologist would not be allowed to speak to the original investigating pathologist for information to enable him to prepare a critique or report of the work done for the court, that he would have to come to court without that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an autopsy carried out in accordance with all the standards and the methodology envisaged for the performance of the autopsy and if this report is decisive, accurate, and clear, and if attached to it there are proper photo files and video recordings, then there is no need for anyone to communicate to anyone. If there is any need or if a new expert in this trial has any objections to the work done or to the autopsy report, then the competent Trial Chamber summons the person who actually conducted the autopsy and calls the witness -- the expert witness who made the objections, and then there is a debate that is moderated by the Trial Chamber, and questions are asked and answers are given to elucidate those doubts, if any. These are the rules that are in place in my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Just one other question. Do you know what the reason is for a rule obliging experts not to communicate with one another prior to a trial?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the systems where there are rules in place to govern the methodology and the procedure, this is legislated, simply -- to put it simply. This is the case in our system, and the fact that the experts cannot communicate is the consequence of the doubt that exists -- that is built into the system in my country into the bias, possible bias of the witness -- of the experts, and that is why they are called to explain any doubts arising from the autopsy report before the Trial Chamber. Because, as you know, in our country, in our legal system, every party -- the parties to the proceedings do not have their experts. The Trial Chamber appoints experts, and they then evaluate the expertise. The parties, the defence counsel of the injured party or of the accused, have the right to seek opinion. They can ask me to provide an opinion, but that is not considered expert testimony. This is my opinion, and the court then evaluates its validity. They can either accept or reject my opinion, or they can summon me to testify. That's up to the Trial Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We are constantly reminding ourselves of the difference between the system here and the system you have in relation to experts. Indeed, I think it was Dr. Tomasevic who actually refused to answer questions here on the basis that they were for an expert only and she wasn't in the context an expert. So it's an issue that poses or presents differences, and differences that it's important that we understand.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Professor Lukic, I'd like to attempt to clarify some points in your expert report. The first question or the first issue I would like you to explain to us is the position and role of the president of the federal government according to the legislation in force from 1994 until the constitutional changes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, your speed is -- has already become an issue, and there's already been a yellow card for talking over the interpretation of the witness's answer, so you're on thin ice already. So you'll need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I won't turn another yellow card, and I'll try to slow down. I hope my question has been interpreted -- no, it hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll need to deal with the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The position of the president of the federal government under the constitutional system of 1992 until the constitutional changes in the year 2000, the influence or effect of the position of the president of the federal government on the way that government made decisions and on its manner of working.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1992 opted for a system of government based on the principle of the division of power, and this follows from the fundamental provisions of this constitution. As it's not usual for a constitution to deal with scholarly and other issues of state organization, this constitution did not go any further in explaining, nor was it its task, what -- in explaining what kind of government authority this was. In order to save time, I won't go into this matter, but I will simply conclude that the legislators who enacted the constitution opted for a well-known type of horizontal organization of central government authority called a chancellor type of government, that is, a government that rests on the so-called chancellor principle. This means that it is a government in which the decisive, the key, role from the moment it is formed until the end is played by its president. In spite of the fact that the federal government consists of the president, the vice-presidents, the federal ministers who are in charge of the ministries, and the federal ministers who are not in charge of federal ministers, in spite of that, in spite of the fact that one might say that the government consisted of several members, the crucial role was played by its president because the only important -- the only thing that was important was that the candidate who was nominated to be the president of the government or the prime minister was elected. Before the candidate came up for election, he was duty-bound to present the programme of his government to the Federal Assembly, and once he was elected, it was considered that the entire cabinet was elected or the entire federal government, and with reference to the aspect I am referring to this was not all that important. If in the course of the life of a government or a cabinet the prime minister decided that changes had to be made in the composition of the cabinet, he would do this of -- on his own initiative, of his own volition, bearing in mind all relevant elements, including his relations with the Federal Assembly, and he would simply inform the Federal Assembly of this, but the Federal Assembly would not issue any decisions concerning this. In addition to this, the prime minister has the right to resign of his own volition when he concludes that this is necessary and no decision is reached in the government, in the cabinet, but only the Federal Assembly -- the Federal Assembly is simply informed of this. The predominant role of the federal prime minister in relation to all the other members of the federal cabinet is also seen from the fact that the constitution expressly provides - and this is shown in my expert report - that the federal prime minister is responsible to the Federal Assembly for his own work and for the work of the federal government. So all this shows that the federal prime minister had a predominant role, so one might conclude that the ministers in the federal cabinet, regardless of their rank or the type of ministers they are, are in a manner of speaking the prime minister's associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Petrovic. It may be my misunderstanding of this, but the transcript says, page 13, line 7: "In spite of the fact that the federal government consists of the president, the vice-presidents, the federal ministers who are in charge of the ministries and the federal ministers who are not in charge of federal ministries, in spite of that, in spite of the fact that one might say the government consisted of several members, the crucial role was played by its president." utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Bonomy mentioned the president of the republic. What was the role of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the process of the election of the federal government, and what was his relation to the federal government and its members?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this, I should say that the main constitutional organs are the Federal Assembly, the president of the republic, the prime minister - as far as I know, prime minister is the only proper translation - and two courts. One of the main constitutional organs is the president of the republic, who according to this constitution has very weak powers, very weak authority, except for his relation to the army. The constitutional relation between the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the federal prime minister refers to only two situations according to the constitution. The first is nominating the candidates for the prime minister, and this is a power that belongs to the president of the republic. However, it should be mentioned that in Yugoslavia at the time there was a multi-party system. The parties competed in the elections, and this power of the president of the FRY was such that he could not act of his own volition. When nominated the candidate for prime minister, he always had to bear in mind the number of seats won by each party in the Federal Assembly because bearing in mind what the majority was in the Federal Assembly, that was the only way he could nominate a candidate for prime minister. Apart from this power of his, the president of the FRY under the constitution of this country had no other legally prescribed powers over the federal government. On the other hand, there was only one power of the federal government in relation to the president of the FRY, and that was that the federal government had expressis verbis, an express authority to propose to the president of the FRY candidates for the post of ambassador. So they could propose what ambassadors would be accredited with other governments or, if need be, with other international organizations, and in this case, also, the president of the republic did not have any powers because the foreign policy fell within the competence of the federal government. So the ambassadors who were nominated were actually implementing the policy of the federal government, and this was prescribed by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you tell us what was -- whether there was any relation between the federal government and the Army of Yugoslavia, and if so, what it was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia was another constitutional organ in the then-FRY, and its legal position was expressly regulated in part 8 of the constitution bearing the title: "The Army of Yugoslavia." The relations between the federal government and the Army of Yugoslavia is something we can draw conclusions about only on the basis of the text of the constitution. If we look at the powers that the federal government has in relation to the army, we may conclude that these were not powers to decide on the use of the Army of Yugoslavia except in one exceptional case, a minor case, and that was that the conduct of foreign policy fell within the remit of the federal government. So the legislator who enacted the constitution empowered the federal government to decide on whether the army would be used for the needs of international organizations, i.e., on peacekeeping missions in other countries. Apart from this power, the federal government had no other powers in relation to the army, especially not as regards command, the internal organization of the Army of Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth. The other powers of the federal government which are prescribed by the constitution are legal powers having to do with the army in the context of preparation for the defence of the country because the federal administration of the federal government prepared a defence plan, but it only had authority over civilian structures in wartime or in the period regulated by norms before a war, and we might say that these were administrative powers in logistical matters. There were no other relations. On the other hand, the Army of Yugoslavia, as is quite normal in democratic countries, has no powers over the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does the federal government have any powers regarding civilian control of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: This is not performed by the government, but rather by the Federal Assembly. The Federal Assembly decides when necessary on the responsibility of the president of the FRY or enacts other legislation having to do with control over the Army of Yugoslavia. So the federal government has no powers falling within the scope of civilian control over the work and activities of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you please tell us something about the relations of the federal government and the republican organs in the republics who were members of the federal state? I'm especially interested in the relations between the federal government and the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Was there any relation between these two organs, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The legislator who enacted the constitution probably had reasons to decide on a type of federation, the type that is prescribed by this constitution. It is characterized by several principles and several fundamental relations. The main principle is that the federal state carries out only those tasks of state government which are linguistically and logically unambiguously assigned to it in the constitution, and this is done by enumerating the powers, and this is a closed list. Apart from the tasks enumerated in the constitution, the federal government cannot undertake any other tasks unless the member republics agree on this, and they did not agree on it while this state lasted. So the fundamental tenet is that the member states are sovereign states, and this is provided for in Article 6 of this constitution; they are sovereign states, and they are sovereign in all issues not expressly put under the -- not expressly assigned to the federal government. There is double track in implementing legislation laws, bylaws, and other legal documents. This constitution provides that the federal state shall implement the federal laws it enacts, and it cannot implement only those federal laws which cannot be implemented directly because, for example, they regulate only the bases of some legal relations, and there were few of these in this constitutional system. This falls to the -- under the so-called mixed or parallel competence, and this has to do with the tax system, the labour system, the social welfare system, and so on and so forth. I won't list them all. On the other hand, the republic in everything that was the task of the government which was not expressly assigned to the federal government was independent, and there were no control mechanisms for the federal government to control this, so these were two separate tracks. Of course, the legislation of the member republics had to comply with the federal constitution, but there were very few principles and very few norms that were binding on the republics. In view of all this, my answer to your question is that the member republics were really independent in carrying out the work falling within its judicial administrative and other competence, and the federal government had no powers of control except for control over legislation and documents, not control over behaviour and activities, and everything else was done by the republics independently. This general rule also applies to the Ministries of the Interior of the member republics, as no organ of the federal government had any legal power over them. The member republics had the right of so-called self-organization, and in this they were bound only by two principles of the federal constitution, that of a civil sovereignty and that of the division of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last subject that I would like us to deal with has to do with Article 99 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, dealing with all the competencies or the powers of the federal government, or rather, Article 77 dealing with the federal organs. In Article 77(1) of the powers of the federal organs is the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas in item 6 there is the power of exercising control over crossing the state border. This was envisaged in the constitution, but was it specified in concrete norms more specifically?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The constitutional legislator practically said what the purview was of the federal state and its organs, and this was done through two procedures. First, in Article 77, the issues and relevant fields were specified that the federal state was in charge of, regulating every one of the powers of each federal organ. Of course, it should be stated that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was -- did not have very long life, historically speaking, and from the point of view of a well-organized or a perfectly organized state, it had not been completed, or rather, it had not been rounded off from a legal point of view. This particularly holds true with regard to two of the questions that you asked me about because Article 77 says that "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, through its organs, establishes or formulates policy, enacts and enforces federal legislation, other laws and general enactments, and ensures judicial protection in various fields." And then it says in item 6: "Border crossing and control of the circulation of goods, services, and passengers across the border." And in item 7, it says that this pertains to the fields of defence and security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as well. Perhaps this would be the right place to point out that the area of defence was regulated, both by laws and bylaws, and that that is where the judiciary, executive, and legislative branches of government function. However, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as we can see, the federal state did not exercise judicial legislative authority, rather, and therefore executive authority wasn't there either. And since both were lacking, then judicial authority could not be exercised in the field of security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia throughout its existence, until it ceased to exist, that is. With regard to all three branches of government, border crossings and the control of circulation of goods, et cetera, everything that is mentioned in this item, was regulated as it was. So that was the destiny of this one particular issue falling under the jurisdiction of the federal state throughout the existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Those were all of our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, I'm afraid I've lost you a little in your last answer where you're dealing with item 7, and you talked about the federal state did not exercise judicial legislative authority, at least that's the English translation. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I will be in a position to clarify this very quickly. As for Article 77 of the constitution, it states that the federal state carries out judicial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got Article 77. It's what you're telling us about that part 7, item 7, in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Item 7 envisages that the federal state has judicial, executive, and legislative authority in the field of security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; however, throughout its existence, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not pass a law on security. Since such a law was not passed, it could not be carried out by the executive, and since it was not being implemented, then there could be no judicial disputes in that area. There was just a single court that existed in this state: The federal court of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was the only one in existence. In other words, the federal state did not exercise its powers in the field of security at all because, in fact, this was carried out by the member republics. I would be very pleased if I managed to explain the essence of this question and the situation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the field of security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Trying to put it into simple layman's language, are you saying that the secret service of Yugoslavia was operated by the various republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yugoslavia didn't have a secret service at all as its own service, as a service of the federal state, as unusual as this may seem to you, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you saying that each republic had one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then every one of the republics carried out this work in relation to its territory, and that is as far as my constitutional law knowledge goes because I am well-versed in constitutional law matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a Federal Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There was never a Federal Ministry of the Interior because, you see, when a prime minister designate would be appointed, then he would decide what the composition of his government would be or his cabinet, to put it in your own linguistic and legal terms. Every prime minister designate did that, but in all the cabinets that were established from 1992 up until the end of the existence of the state union, there was no Federal Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, no doubt, but I have a recollection that Mr. Bulatovic, when here, told us that there was a Ministry of the Interior of sorts in the federal government, but that's not your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it did exist -- well, you really caught me by surprise now. I cannot remember because at that time I did not live in Serbia. At any rate, it was not involved in carrying out security work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So throughout the Federation, how were the activities of the security services coordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I would be best placed to answer that question because as for police coordination and police work, indeed, I never dealt with such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to start with a couple of questions about your CV, which I understand is annex 4 to your report, and it's our Exhibit Number 2D394. In looking at your work history, I seem to have a gap between 25 May 1992 and 25 October 1993. Can you tell us what you were doing during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, unfortunately, I was not in a position to pursue my academic or research career because due to the war operations in Sarajevo where I lived and worked at the law school of the University of Sarajevo, my university career was interrupted. From May 1992 until October 1993 I was unemployed, but during that period of time at the request of people that I had cooperated with before the war, I was legal advisor but without having established formal employment with Professor Dr. Aleksa Buha, who was then foreign minister of Republika Srpska. In that period of time I was also legal advisor, upon invitation, of the delegation of Republika Srpska that negotiated in Geneva under the auspices of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia. All of this, due to the fact that from 1991 I took part as a representative of the Serb side from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the work of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia that started working precisely here, in The Hague, and later on continued working in Brussels and ultimately in Geneva. So that is the void, as it were, that you referred to, whereas the CV states only matters of relevance to my academic and researcher status, not only to -- it was not done to avoid things, but I thought that I should only give references that qualified me as an expert in constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, and I trust you'll understand that I'm asking these questions to determine if there's anything that may bear on credibility or bias or some motive to testify a particular way. I had a note somewhere that listed you as a deputy minister for foreign affairs for the Republika Srpska in 1994. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed. First, you asked me about the period from 1992 and 1994, and I responded; now you're asking me about the period from 1994. Yes, from October - I don't know exactly when, October 20-something - I was deputy foreign minister of Republika Srpska all the way up to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say from October. Is that October 1993 or October 1994 that you achieved that position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: 1994 at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that a paid position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It was so well paid that I had to work in Belgrade in order to feed my family, so that I could work for free in Pale. Even if it had been paid -- I mean, people who were paid for work there could not live off that money. Just as a matter of curiosity, people who worked as deputy ministers had a salary of 10 euro in present-day terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that per month or per year?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Per month. I, in order to feed my family and myself, worked at the Institute for Comparative Law in Belgrade, which is a research institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: During a certain period of time, six or seven years, I'm not sure, I was a member of the Serb Democratic Party. I left the party in 1992. I can't remember the exact date, but let's say it was the month of April because that year I competed in order to become a judge of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and one of the requirements for that job was that the candidate involved was not a member of a single political party. So for five or six or seven years - I can't tell you exactly - I was a member of this party. If I give it some more thought, I may be able to tell you. I think it was from 1996 -- now, was it 1996 -- until April 1992 [as interpreted]. That is when I resigned from the main committee of the Serb Democratic Party for the reasons that I've just explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you not again after --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Could my learned friend Mr. Hannis put the question regarding the duration of his membership in the Serb Democratic Party. I think that the answer is a bit confusing. The transcript is not [as interpreted] confusing. From 1996 until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until April 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that time-period from 1996 to 2002, did you hold any positions within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: From 1996 until 2002, I think that it was only from 1998 that I was a member of the Main Board, as I said to you, and then I left it in April 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was the party that was founded by Radovan Karadzic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: That is a party that was founded at its founding assembly in Sarajevo. I did not attend. Many people founded it. Radovan Karadzic was not the only man who founded it. The founding meeting was held, as far as I know, in a big sports hall of the biggest sports centre of Sarajevo, Skenderija, that could take 6 or 7.000 people at a time. This is what people told me about. The hall was full, so there were many people who founded that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My point is, though, that that's the party that is primarily associated with Radovan Karadzic and generally viewed or termed a Serb nationalist party, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I really cannot state any views on that, and I did not look at how people were characterizing it. Some people characterize it this way; some people characterize it that way. At any rate, this is not a question that I would need to answer. This is a statement made by the person who was actually putting that by way of a question in terms of what he believes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're not aware that the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina during President Karadzic's time in that position was viewed as a nationalist Serb party? You must have been aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me make one thing clear. I understand English quite well, but I am listening to my language because one feels the best in one's own language. I don't know whether the interpretation I received was correct, but it said that the Serbian Democratic Party was a nationalist party and was viewed as a nationalist Serb party. I can tell you only this. You can talk about various qualifications. You asked me whether I was aware of that, but I can tell you this. At that time, I paid very little attention to labels, to how things were called, because one had to make a living and survive. Now, as to the second part of your question, whether I was aware of the fact that it was a nationalist party, it of course gathered around it mostly Serbs, but it was not by any means the only party in Bosnia and Herzegovina that had Serb membership, that attracted Serbs, if by that you mean that most of its members were of the Serbian ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what would you describe as its primary platform in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: How would I describe its platform, its primary platform? As far as I know, I share those views, I and the party, although I was not a member, supported it because it expressed the interests of the great majority of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They wanted to retain the joint state, to restructure it to the degree that it was possible, and to do that in -- by peaceful means and without any blood. This is what I knew about the Serbian Democratic Party at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it, then, that you wouldn't know whether the HDZ was viewed as a Croatian nationalist party or the SDA was viewed as a Muslim nationalist party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you the same answer as I did about the Serbian Democratic Party. What is clear and evident and -- both to me and to everybody else in that area was that the Croatian Democratic Union gathered in the overwhelming majority Croats, people of Croat ethnic background in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the same went for the Party of Democratic Action, which gathered around it Muslims, or as they are now defined in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosniaks. This is a fact that cannot be denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You say that you were a professor at the Serb Sarajevo law faculty from 1 November 1999. Are you still a member of that law faculty?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I continued my university career. I resumed it in November 1999. I no longer work there. Throughout this period, I was the dean and the professor. I taught constitutional law and political system, and I was fired on the 16th of January, 2006, so it's been two years and a half - how time flies - because the decision of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 30th of June, 2004, was being implemented, removing me from the position of the member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. I was not a member of that board at all at that time, but this imprecision does not really concern me because many other people were also fired, and some of them were characterized or mistaken for some other people who simply shared the same name, and the Office of the High Representative then made this mistake. They said I was a member of the Main Board of the SDS, although I was not, and they also prohibited me from taking any public office. I was prohibited from being a member of any political party. I was prohibited from participating in any elections as a candidate. So I was prohibited from taking any public office that would be funded by the budget. So as the university professor, I could not work in any service that was financed from the budget of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I could not get a job as a cleaner, as a driver, anything. Of course, all this was the consequence of the enforcement of this decision, and I was not even informed that proceedings had been instituted against me. I was not aware of any accusations levied against me. I think that you will find this decision, and you will not be able to find any act that would constitute a criminal offence on my part, and what was done to me actually amounted to a criminal sanction. I think that now I've given you my answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and it raises a few more questions for me. There is a decision from 30 June 2004 by Paddy Ashdown as the High Commissioner to remove you from your position as a member of the Main Board of the SDS. You're telling us you were no longer a member of the Main Board at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was not a member of the Main Board. Had any proceedings been instituted against me by the Office of the High Representative, they would have been able to determine that fact very easily because in the Serbian Democratic Party archives, there is a letter in which I informed the president of the party that I resign from my position in the board and that I no longer want to be a member because I wanted to apply for the post at the constitutional court and -- but no proceedings had been instituted, and this was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was not done? Your resignation was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: My resignation was accepted, and after that I did not participate in the work of the Serbian Democratic Party and its Main Board because first I was appointed a judge of the constitutional court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then the High Representative cancelled this appointment on the basis of a request by the Bosniak representatives in the Constitutional Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was a member of that commission too. But I was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party Main Board at that time, so there could be no debate about any acceptance or not acceptance because it -- this was my personal action. But if any proceedings had been instituted against me or if any procedure was done to check these facts, then they would have found that out, but this was simply not done. They did not check the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you try to seek any relief from that decision through some legal proceeding?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course. I did not appeal against this decision with the High Representative because no proceedings in which I participated were actually conducted, and if there were no proceedings then I could not appeal with any other body, external body. These are the basic tenets of legal procedure that I taught my students. Out of the 59, 26 of us filed a complaint before the European Court of Human Rights because the rest of the people from that group of 59 were very much afraid that they might face harsher sanctions than the ones that they got, and these sanctions were imposed without any legal norms and without any legal proceedings. The 26 were brave enough. We were brave enough to do that, if you can call that bravery, of course, because this is a basic expression of your self-esteem. And European Court of Human Rights recently issued a decision rejecting our complaint. We, of course, filed suit against Bosnia and Herzegovina for failing to fulfil its obligations under Article 1 related to Article 6 of the European Charter -- I'm sorry, not 6 but 7 of the European Charter of Human Rights, and the European Court of Human Rights decided that it lacked jurisdiction because this action could not be attributed to Bosnia and Herzegovina but to the High Representative, and the High Representative in making this decision did not perform any of the tasks of the sovereign government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; but, as is indicated explicitly in the decision of the court, it had the authority of the UN Security Council. On the other hand, I filed three suits before national courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina; one is the legal suit about the fact that I was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And none of those have been resolved yet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: In one of them I have the first-instance judgement, and the first-instance court ruled in my favour, ordering the faculty to give me back my job and to pay both the damages, but the faculty appealed against this judgement. And there were also two administrative proceedings before the district court in Banja Luka. In the first case, the court decided it was not an administrative case and that there could be no administrative proceedings. In the second one, it ruled in my favour because it decided that the Government of Republika Srpska did not have the authority to remove from office a dean of a faculty and to appoint somebody else to that post. These were legal suits that I filed in order to protect my rights. Of course, now we're talking about filing suit before appropriate bodies of the United Nations because we cannot see how it is that the bodies of the United Nations can violate their own basic documents such as the Declaration of Human Rights, which has become part of international law, and how two covenants on human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was, are any of those finally resolved, or are they still pending on appeal or at some other stage of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Appellate proceedings are now underway in the administrative proceedings and in the proceedings before the court. Well, when we're talking about administrative proceedings, we're talking about different kind of relief, but that's basically it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I have one other question dealing with this general topic before I go to ask you about your report. I furnished to the Defence counsel yesterday some open-source news articles about you that I might ask a question about. I don't know if you were shown that or you're aware of it, but one is a story from the Pale Javnost publication on the 13th of July, 1996, which purports to be an interview with you where you are described as the deputy foreign affairs minister of the Serb Republic, and you're being interviewed by someone named Jovan Janjic. Do you recall that interview?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I know Jovan Janjic. He's a journalist. He used to be an editor in Javnost magazine, and if you remind me, I will be able to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in English, the title of the article: "Serb Official On Achieving Strategic Balance," and he's asking -- he's describing or talking about a conference on arms control and Vienna among other things. Do you remember being interviewed about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was the head of the delegation of the Republika Srpska at the talks about the implementation of the annex 1, I think, to the Dayton Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: That's arms control, regional stabilization, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in the article, he mentions that you've also been to Brussels, The Hague, London, and Geneva, and taking part in various negotiations, including the final negotiations in Dayton, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was a member of the delegation of Republika Srpska during proximity talks in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you read this article at the time it came out, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, try and jog my memory, and if I'm able to recall I will talk about that because I don't have any details in my life that I would like to keep secret. I didn't give many interviews. I didn't write a lot, but a long time has passed, so I can't really recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just two parts I want to ask you about. In the first paragraph, he describes you as the deputy foreign affairs minister, and he says that you have "been a part of the Serb nationalist movement from the very beginning." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serb nationalist movement or national movement -- yes, you can say that in a way because as an expert for constitutional law, I took part in the talks under the auspices of the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia, the International Conference for Yugoslavia first and then for the former Yugoslavia, so that's the time-period 1991/1992; and these were my duties mostly until 1998, which was the time until which I worked as the deputy foreign minister of Republika Srpska. So you could say that I was a member of that movement. I think in 1996, I became a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. Now, I cannot really interpret the journalist's thoughts or ideas because these are not my words. These are his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me ask you one last thing before the break, if I may, which reflects your words. The question from Mr. Janjic was: "What do you as a legal specialist think about The Hague trial of Serb leaders?" You said, according to him: "It is completely clear that this is an attempt to break the morale and ethics of the Serb nation and place it at the very bottom of the historical and civilizational pit; an attempt to drive the Serb nation to self-hatred and create in it a feeling of the absurdity of its own existence and the futility of any struggle. Also, it is an attempt to decapitate the Serb nation in the Serb republic by destroying its leaders. It seems that someone has to replace Germany and the German people in that historic role. Numerous legal and political problems of that Tribunal and the trial itself have still not been resolved. It's impossible to make the Serb nation guilty of genocide because it was defending itself there and had no intention of destroying other nations; it never did. This holds true for its political and military leaders. I think that this completely senseless and pale attempt at a rerun of Nuremberg will not succeed." That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, this sounds like some of the views that I expressed, and I don't want to keep it a secret. Now, whether I phrased it quite exactly in those terms I can't tell you, but for the most part this corresponds to my views of some elements of the pre-war, war, and post-war developments in these areas. And of course, I'm doing this as a free man because freedom of thought for me and even in areas where there is none is the basic prerequisite for any other freedom and for a free society, so this does sound like my views. Now, whether this is really what I said or whether he really transposed my words the way that I said them, I don't know that. You may know that unfortunately newspaper articles and interviews are rarely authenticated or reviewed before publishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a good time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is. Professor, we need to have a break at this stage. It's routine. It's for 20 minutes. Could you leave the courtroom, please, with the usher while we have this break, and we'll resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, now I want to turn to your report, which is our Exhibit 2D239, I believe, and I want to talk first about annex 1, which has to do with territorial autonomy. This is kind of complex and difficult for me to follow, so I'll try to ask you just a few questions in layman's terms. Would it be fair to say that between 1968 and prior to 1988 that the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina enjoyed a very high level of autonomy, so high, in fact, that they were pretty much on an equal footing with the republics in the former Yugoslavia? Or is that too simplistic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, as usual, if it's simple, it's bound to be complicated. Let me try and sum up in the briefest possible terms as follows: Perhaps we should first address the issue of what autonomy is, whether there is a universal type of autonomy, whether there is one measure, one content that would allow us to measure all the other phenomena that could be termed autonomy. But it would be pointless in this case. All I'm trying to stress here is that there is a problem of how one understands it, even if we use the same terms. If you allow me, I will answer. A famous professor, we share the same name, he was famous and very prominent in the former Yugoslavia. He said always whenever there was a debate, Our first task is to define the terms lest we should use the same words to talk about different things or different words to talk about the same things. And you could say that the autonomous province of Vojvodina and the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija and then later on Kosovo in the period that you referred to - well, that period could further be divided into subperiods - did have the constitutional position that in some respects was similar to those of other units, similar but not the same. I say that advisedly because although there were similarities, there were also some differences. Only federal units under the constitutions that were in force in Yugoslavia at that time were entitled to self-determination. Of course, the issue was what the right to self-determination entails, whether it entails the right to secession. Similar to that was the constitutional position of peoples and ethnic minorities. Of course, we could talk about the relationship between the Socialist Republic of Serbia, as the federal was called at that time, and the socialist autonomous provinces that were part of it, and we could also conclude that there was a high degree of similarity with some differences. So there was a high degree of similarity but there were some fundamental differences, the key being the fact that the territorial and political autonomies, the two that existed in Serbia, did not have the right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But during that period, the autonomous provinces each had their own constitution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Not from the beginning, only at a later stage. First, they had the constitutional laws when the 1968 constitution was amended, and then they were given right to their own constitutions. I do apologise for this correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this time-period they also -- and I'm primarily interested in Kosovo, obviously. They primarily got the right to have their own Supreme Court, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, under the 1974 constitution, that is correct. They had the right to set up their own courts as part of their judiciary government in the territory of their province, which was in accordance with the way in which the state then was organized.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this time-period, Kosovo had its own assembly and own Executive Council, which had the right to initiate proceedings before the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have the right to initiate proceedings in certain cases before the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia and the Constitutional Court of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at page 14 of your report in English, you talk about the province got basically the right of veto regarding changes or amendments to the federal constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In this aspect their position was the same as the position of the federal units because the SFRY constitution could only be amended with the approval of the assemblies of the republics and of the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on page 16 in the English of your report, you talk about "Since they now were able to participate in changing the SFRY constitution on the principle of unanimity, the provinces like the republics have ultimate responsibility, which is the most important component of the right to self-organizing." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just read it first. I do apologise. I'm just checking to verify. What do you mean the responsibility? The responsibility of which the most important component was the right -- which responsibility are you referring to, the ultimate responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm just reading the English translation. It says: "And since they participate in changing" -- and I don't know what the B/C/S page is. Maybe Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, you can say it in English. Please, do say it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In English, it says: "And since they participate in changing" --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me the paragraph and the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. On page 16 of the English. It's the second paragraph, and it's the last sentence in that paragraph. Do you find it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] "And since they participated ..." [Interpretation] Is it that one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. And there's a reference to "ultimate responsibility" there.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me compare it to see whether the translation is correct because there are usually problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 22, first paragraph in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the translation is not correct. The translation is not correct, the English translation. In fact, I used the term "kompetenz" from the German legal theory. I think that there is a similar legal term in the English language. So they have the jurisdiction to have jurisdiction. Under the German theory of federalism, that would pertain only to the federal state. Here, it went one level down to the federal unit and the autonomous province. It's a mistake in translation, but you can't really blame the translators because these are technical terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, would you now read the sentence in B/C/S slowly, and we'll have it clarified by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And since they participate in amending the SFRY constitution on the principle of unanimity, the provinces have, as do the republics, the competence of the competence, "nadleznost nadleznosti," which is the most important component of the right to self-organizing. "So the autonomous province has the competence of the competence over itself, which is atypical. If you do a comparative study of various forms of autonomy, there is no historical precedent in which an autonomy has this "kompetenz kompetenz" kind of competence to decide on how it would organize itself. Everywhere, it is connected to the state, and it is the state that prescribes how the political and territorial autonomy will be organized. It is the competence of the state. It does so in its constitution or by its constitution and laws. Unlike this solution, which is quite usual, there are some" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just wanted a translation. Thank you very much. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. The point I'm trying to get to is that from this position that existed in Kosovo and Metohija prior to 1989, this high level of -- what I call this high level of autonomy, there were changes made in the constitution of Serbia, and then there were the events on the 23rd of March, 1989, in the Assembly in Kosovo. And after that, Kosovo had what I would call a much reduced level of autonomy. Would you agree with that general statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, again, I can say that sometimes we're using the same words to refer to different things. In 1988, changes were made -- or rather, amendments were made to the SFRY constitution, and some of these amendments concerned the position of the provinces in the Republic of Serbia. These amendments to the federal constitution were made precisely for the reason -- or rather, precisely in order to eliminate elements blocking the legislative and executive power in the Republic of Serbia in relation to Article 301 of the constitution referring to laws enacted by Serbia for the territory of the entire republic. The goal of these amendments - and this was beyond dispute - was to remove impermissible blockades in the functioning of the republics so that amendments were made to the Serbian constitution, and there were many amendments, but only four or five related to the status of the autonomous provinces within Serbia. And it was stated there that the position of the province in the Federation cannot be changed by that constitution, but the position of the province within Serbia was changed, which actually got Serbia out of this situation where its work was being blocked so that judicial control of laws and bylaws on the territory of all of Serbia was put in place. Nowhere is it written down that this part of the position of the autonomous provinces within Serbia is inalterable, nor is it guaranteed as a right, and it was Serbia that had the "kompetenz kompetenz" power in relation to the organization of its state government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But would you not agree with me that a reasonable outside observer would look at the difference between 1998 and 1990 and say that Kosovo, the province, does not have the same level of autonomy that it had earlier, that it has been reduced. Can you agree with that general proposition?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Even an unreasonable observer could notice that there had been a change, but anyone versed in the problems of constitutional law could not say that autonomy had been reduced because the kind of autonomy - and let me use your expression rather than mine - the kind of autonomy that existed in constitutional and legal terms was atypical for both provinces. There were not many such experiences with federalism and regionalism, so serious evaluation would be that the contents of the political territorial autonomy under the amendments of 1988 and 1989 and the federal and republican constitution were reduced within -- to within the reasonable limits of what was known and what had already been seen in constitutional law [as interpreted]. In any case, it's correct that the provinces did not have some of the powers they had had before, but I would not agree with you that their autonomy had been reduced. It was only that something that in comparative legal terms had been warped or overemphasized in that autonomy was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, page 44, line 13, the professor said what was already seen in comparative constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor, maybe it's a matter of semantics, but if money is withdrawn from my bank account, I view my bank account as being reduced. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: This was not a provincial bank account that could be reduced. They had more -- they had been given more, actually, than they should have had. So these are two different situations, and we can't view them in the same terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this way. After 1990, was Kosovo permitted to have a constitution of its own? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Kosovo permitted to have its constitution? Well, Kosovo had its statute, which was the legal document pertaining to its organization. Likewise, Vojvodina, as you view it, did not have the right to its own constitution, and it enacted a statute, and it was quite peaceful until -- well, it has been peaceful up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. But before 1988, Kosovo was permitted to have a constitution; after 1990, they only had a statute, not a constitution, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to bear in mind when drawing this comparison that Kosovo had had a statute before that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Please, just try to answer my questions. I'll try to keep them simple. Before 1989, during that time-period between 1974 and 1989, Kosovo was permitted to have a Supreme Court, but after 1990, they were not, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, but Kosovo hadn't had the Supreme Court before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You answered my question when you said "of course." I'm talking about what level of autonomy they had, what things they had prior to 1990 that they no longer had after 1990. After 1990, they no longer -- Kosovo no longer had the right of veto of the federal constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: After 1990, after 1990, Kosovo did have the right of veto to the federal constitution for as long as the federal constitution applied. But the problems were of a different nature then because the federal state was not functioning at the time for reasons which are probably not of interest in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You then talk about the period in the autonomous provinces in 1998 [sic] to 1990 at page 20 of the English, and the first paragraph, you say: "The position, organization, and role of territorial autonomies in the constitutional order of Yugoslavia and Serbia, the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, the Constitution of Vojvodina and Kosovo, which were adopted in 1974, elicited numerous and various debates and demands for change." And based on what you described earlier in your report and what you told us, I can well imagine that that did happen, and that's what led to the events that led to what you talk about, the withdrawal of autonomy, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean withdrawal of autonomy? What point of time are you referring to, and what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The changes that occurred as a result of the changes to the Constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: What year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 1989 amendments and the vote that took place in the Kosovo Assembly on March 23rd.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The amendments of 1989 did not withdraw autonomy. Kosovo continued to have the status of a political and territorial autonomy, just as Vojvodina did, but with reduced competencies corresponding to the actual position of these two provinces, which with some small differences corresponded to what they had had prior to 1968. One could [as interpreted] say that the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija had been withdrawn if Kosovo and Metohija had ceased to exist or if it ceased to have the kind of rights that belonged to autonomous provinces generally. So I cannot agree with you when you say that territorial autonomy was withdrawn by the amendments of 1989 because it simply does not correspond to the truth when one looks at the theoretical thought about the position of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. 47, 5, 6, it is obvious that from the context of the answer this doesn't make sense: One can say that the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija had been withdrawn. I believe witness said quite contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: One cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness should be instructed to talk slower so the interpreters can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter has corrected it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank Professor, I stopped you because I don't believe in my question I used the term "territorial autonomy." Let me ask you, though, in your report on page 22 where you're talking about the autonomous provinces in the constitutional order of the Republic of Serbia since 1990, the last sentence in that first paragraph says: "According to the Constitution of Serbia, Article 6, in the Republic of Serbia there exists the autonomous province of Vojvodina and the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija as forms of territorial autonomy." Can you give me a brief description of what territorial autonomy means. Does that just mean you have a border that can't be changed, or is it something more?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: There's an express provision in article 6 of the constitution, which says that: "In the Republic of Serbia, there is the autonomous province of Vojvodina and the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija as forms of territorial autonomy." In comparative constitutional law, it's usual for the very existence of autonomy to be established by the constitution because, thereby, the highest legal guarantee is provided of its existence because there is no law higher than the constitution. And, likewise, there is no greater guarantee than the one provided by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the guarantee is for territorial autonomy. My question was: What is territorial autonomy? Does that just mean you have a nonviolable border that can't be changed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Territorial autonomy rarely in the world means that there are borders which cannot be violated or changed. The unchangeable borders of territorial autonomy do not exist anywhere. There can only be a provision stating that the territory of a political territorial autonomy can be changed only with the agreement of the autonomy itself. But in constitutional history, there is no example of an autonomy, with one exception up north in history, which had certain elements, but there is no example of a territory being unalterable as regards its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me what the term "territorial autonomy" means in Article 6 of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia? What does that mean for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: For Kosovo, it means what is in norms 108, 109, 110, 111, and 112 of this constitution because the norm in Article 6, the provision in Article 6, has a principled nature. It's a general nature, so the initial provisions are general provisions, and then after that in section 6 entitled "Territorial Organization," the first part, the first subsection is entitled: "The Autonomous Province of Vojvodina and The Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija," and that is what is meant by a legislator when he guaranteed the existence of the autonomy in Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait. You understand the answer, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not just mean that there's autonomy on a certain territory? I'm reluctant to put words in the witness's mouth when he's been asked the question a number of times. Can you not help Mr. Hannis by just telling him what territorial autonomy means as a concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that is listed in these provisions, Articles 108 to 112, the concept of a political territorial autonomy, is reached in the following way: The position of certain territories in a certain state is compared on the one hand with the position of the federal units in the state, if they exist, or if they exist in the world comparatively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've now answered it, and it does say on page 16 in the English, Mr. Hannis: "On its territory, the province is the alter-ego of the republic ..." So it does appear that territorial is simply an indicator of the territory over which autonomy is exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to move on, Professor, to what's annex 2 of your report. This is the portion dealing with the federal cabinet in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and in your introductory paragraph you explain that your analysis in paragraph 4 -- you explain your analysis will be carried out using the legal dogmatic method, and in the last paragraph under that introduction section, you say: "Other methods of analysis can only be second rate and supplemental." You mention the Anglo-American legal system where the necessary reliability and precision of conclusions is achieved by the primary use of non-legal methods requiring the method of analysis to be absolutely adapted to the subject of analysis." Maybe I'm biassed. That sounds like a good approach to me. What's wrong with that approach?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not just that. In European continental law when such matters are analysed, the primary thing is the legal source or the legal regulation. It is studied by the dogmatic legal method. So first, its meaning is studied, possible meanings are sought, and one meaning is selected. In European continental law and its system of education, for example, you will find that constitutional law is studied much more using the text of the constitution and so-called organic laws, whereas in the USA, if you are from the USA you will know that it is studied more from the decisions of the constitutional court. Also, you will find there that the court in the USA, especially the courts when they are carrying out constitutional control, they say that there are political questions that the court will not deal with. You will not find such a situation before the constitutional courts in continental Europe because the legal dogmatic or legal normative method is primarily applied. So these are different legal civilizations or legal cultures. It's not a matter of one being superior to the other. It's like the old discussion as to whether it's better to create law by legislation or by precedent. That is a discussion which I think is out of place here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move, then, to section 2 where you talk about the position and the federal cabinet in the organization of the government in the federal republic. In the first paragraph, you mention eight -- in addition to the federal cabinet eight explicitly named state organs starting with the Federal Assembly and so on. You say that "In addition to these nine in total explicitly named and established state organs, the constitution also establishes several generic and functionally defined state organs called ministries, whose exact number and exact competence are not established in advanced and permanently, but rather depend on the federal cabinet." So, for example, we know that at various times in Yugoslavia there was a Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Ministry of Justice, a Ministry of Defence. Are those not permanent ministries and they only appear depending on the particular federal cabinet that's in power?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The answer to your question lies in the following explanation. Tradition, or rather, the tradition of constitutional legal regulation in the second Yugoslavia from 1945 to 1992 was in one period that the constitution expressly prescribes the number and kind of federal ministries, and later on this was abandoned, and then the number and kind of federal ministries was regulated by law. Therefore, in establishing the organization of executive -- of the executive government, the fundamental role was played by the legislative government [as interpreted]. Why? Because in that period in Yugoslavia, state authority was founded on the principle of the unity of government in the hands of the legislative body, the representative body. The constitution of 1992 rests on the principle of the division of power and on the chancellor principle. The influence of the legislative government on the forming and establishing of the executive government should not have been large. Any federal prime minister could -- I'll answer your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... well, I'm not sure you are. I just asked are those not permanent ministries, and do they only appear depending on the particular federal cabinet that's in power? Maybe I should break it in two parts. Are those not permanent ministries?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not what it's about. Every federal minister could introduce a new ministry or abolish an existing ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even -- wait, wait --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even one of the eight or nine explicitly named bodies, or are those not ministries?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to? What bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What you referred to as explicitly named state organs. So I guess the federal state prosecutor is not a ministry, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So those could not be --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those specifically named constitutional bodies could not be abolished by the cabinet or the prime minister, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, because there's the division of power. When you say division of power or the branches of government, this cannot influence the judicial, executive, and legislative branch of government. So the state organs that are named are constitutional organs, and the executive authority was in the hands of the federal government. The ministries and other federal organs and organizations, what it says here is the federal ministries, the federal organs and organizations. It doesn't say that by chance because in Serbia - and that's how it was in Montenegro and still is - there are three kinds of administrative organs who are not exercising executive power. They have an administrative function, and these are ministries, independent and non-independent federal organs, and the so-called independent administrative organizations. They are there to implement the laws, to implement legislation. Their number and kind depends on the acts of the federal government. The federal government has the right to organize itself as the executive branch of government. It can say how many ministries and how many administrative bodies and independent administrative organizations there will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You list --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have an intervention in the transcript before we move on. It's 52, lines 14 and 19. Instead of legislative government, it should be legislative body, because that is what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in that Article 2, you list the eight other explicitly named state organs, and on page 5 of the English in this report, you say: "Based on the aforementioned constitutional provision, it can be concluded that no federal organ has a dominant role over another." And I take it you mean based on what it says on paper, but in real life in 1998 and in 1999 that was not the case in the FRY, was it? Did not the president of the republic, Mr. Milosevic, have a dominant role over some of those other state organs, like the Yugoslav Army, the Supreme Defence Council, the national bank? I'm talking about de facto power.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Legal norms were the subject of my expertise, regulating questions pertaining to political territorial autonomy and questions related to the position of the federal government and also its relations with other constitutional and legal organs. So in terms of factual questions, in terms of how power was exercised, I did not deal with that, I did not prepare to speak about that, and after all, I'm not methodologically equipped to deal with it here and now, this particular question. So even though I have the best of intentions, I cannot give you an answer to that question because it goes beyond my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you as a non-expert and as a citizen who lived in the territory or in the area at the time. Can you answer it that way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I did not live in that area at the time. I lived in Pale, near Sarajevo, and I worked there. Secondly, I am giving answers here as an expert, not as a citizen. I hope that you understand my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, are you -- if the Judge asked you to answer the question, would you provide the answer, then, as a non-expert, or are you refusing to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: If the honourable Judge asked me, I would give the same answer because this is the subject of my testimony. I did not come here as a fact witness; I came here to testify about facts pertaining to law, legal facts based on legal norms, I could say, conditionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no point in my remaining silent on this at the moment because I have a list of questions which will tread into actuality rather than theory, and you're telling us now that you won't be prepared to answer these questions.
