For example, I'll be interested to look at what appears to be the position in theory as contrasted with what might appear to have been the position in practice, and you say you would not deal with that sort of question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand my testimony and the invitation addressed to me by the Defence, I am dealing with these major constitutional law issues. I really did not study those questions and those relations that the honoured Prosecutor is talking about, so that is the truth. If I was called here as an expert on norms and the system, it would be proper for me to give answers to that. I was not called here, and that wasn't the subject of my expertise, either, to compare the normative and the actual. After all, that would be a major expertise that could not be carried out by one person, but rather an entire team of people, and this expertise would take a rather long time if one wanted to be serious about it and close to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me take the blame --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do we need to have the witness leave the room?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. So let me take the blame for this. I intentionally asked for an expert outside the territory of Serbia, or rather, Yugoslavia who knows about constitutional matters so that he could tell us what it should have been like. According to the system that I work in, you will establish what things actually were. Now, if my thinking was erroneous, then I'm to be blamed because there are so many professors in five or six law schools at universities in Serbia, and they could have all come here as expert witnesses; however, I chose, an expert witness so that we would have a clear-cut situation as to what it is supposed to be like. Unfortunately, we are all aware of what it was like. So that is for you to establish. That is what I thought. So mea culpa, the witness did not live in Serbia at the time or in Montenegro, for that matter. Mea culpa, as we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Let me give you an example, Professor. You've told us that under the FRY constitution, the president of the FRY had very few powers. Now, as a matter of fact in the period from 1997 onwards, do you accept that the most powerful person in Yugoslavia was Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, as a researcher, as a university professor, I was taught to utter my judgements very cautiously when I'm trying to deal with research and when I'm involved in scholarly matters. Of course that I can give you an answer straight away, this or that kind of answer, but that would be mere speculation. In order to give an answer to that question, I would have to look at a series of documents from these or other archives. I would have to look at correspondence, programmes, documents, and it is only then that I could answer that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you another way just as a citizen of the world. Do you accept that world leaders at that time regarded Slobodan Milosevic as the most powerful person in Yugoslavia, rightly or wrongly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read in the newspapers something along those lines, but I did not talk to any one of them. I did not talk to foreign diplomats about that question, so I did not participate in that kind of international politics. So at this point in time I'm not qualified to discuss the matter in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there is an issue that does concern this Tribunal, which doesn't live in the theoretical world but tries to live in the real world. And if there is a perception in the world in general that he is Mr. Yugoslavia and you are a constitutional law expert that considers that the terms of the constitution give him limited powers, do you not think it is a legitimate question to be put to you as an expert: How could it be that he could wield power way beyond that provided in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can discuss that with you only in the domain of norms and examples. Now, whether I am good-looking and strong, well, somebody may say that I am, and others may say I'm not. If you're talking about the powers that Mr. Milosevic exercised when he was president of the republic, I do beg your pardon, Your Honour, but then you have to tell me what this is exactly about, whether this does fall under a norm, and then I will tell you whether that is in accordance with the constitution. However, that is only the language and the terrain of legal documents. However, as for this kind of analysis and expertise, I did not prepare for that because the Defence did not ask me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered my question, but insofar as your answer may have a bearing on the question, are you saying that my -- that to pose the question I posed would not be legitimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean to me as an expert witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- regarding these two questions and the norms related to that? I hope that you will understand that what my belief is exactly what you said, precisely due to the subject matter that I'm providing expertise on. By your leave, it would be legitimate to put the question to me in the following way: A document is shown to me, and then I try to give my estimate and say whether that is within the constitution or not. All the rest is really speculation. Sometimes it seemed to me that some of my professors were very wise, and later on when I matured myself, I realized that they were not as smart as I thought they were although they were smart. Now, it's a question of moment; it's a question of impression. However, we are trying to go into serious analysis here. If you tell me Slobodan Milosevic passed a law and said that was the law and then you asked me whether that was in accordance with the constitution, I will say straight away no because the president of the republic is not entitled to exercise judicial authority. That's the kind of analysis I'm prepared to go into because that is why I am here. As for beyond that, I cannot answer questions like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it follow from what you've said so far that you cannot say that the conduct of President Milosevic throughout his period in power fell within the terms of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you will have to tell me what you mean exactly, what legal document. I can only talk about documents. Lawyers deal with power, and political sociologists deal with might. I'm a lawyer. Power or might can be exercised in different ways, as influence, but I did not go into that kind of analysis. I only deal with analysis through law and through the language of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to, Professor, ask you a question in a more simpler way to understand and appreciate what may be your information. Now, you're telling us about those limitations which are enshrined in the constitution with respect to the powers of the president. Okay. These are now laid, enshrined in the constitution. Well, there is another issue, whether the president kept himself within the periphery of those limitations or did he transcend and overstep. Have you any information on that? Did he keep himself within those limitations or he did not; he overstepped, circumvented, cut corners here and there. Can you speak on that subject, or you cannot? I mean, this may help us in appreciating the realism of the constitution and not what is just the black-lettered words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except for legal sources, or rather, the constitution that is attached to certain laws and some bylaws, I did not study documentation or archives about the work of these organs. I did not study any documents of any kind pertaining to the mutual relations among these organs. So, quite simply, I do not have that kind of information in my hands. Finally, the Defence told me that I was not called for that kind of expertise. No documents of that kind were placed before me, and there was no agreement to that effect, that I would be providing expertise on that. So, quite simply, I don't have that. As for my own impressions about this or that person, I really wouldn't go into that. That's not what I do as an individual let alone as a researcher. This is the way I act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Anybody who claims himself to be an expert on the constitution shall also speak about whether the constitution was being followed or it was not being followed because obviously when he's reading the constitution he's also reading the areas where it was followed or where it was not followed. That was the simple question because anybody -- all the constitutional experts you would see who have written books on constitution would say, Well, this was being followed or this was not being followed. This is the law whether they adhered to it or didn't adhere to it. General way. It's nothing to be specific about nor to place you in any difficulty. If you have a view, good enough; if you say, well, you are oblivious to all that unless you see that, then what have you been reading to be an expert to tell us whether this in reality was something followed that way? I mean, this is something which bothers me a little, if you can speak on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat what I have already said, but I'm not going to do that because that is pointless, isn't it? I repeat, I did not have this kind of documentation before me. I was not looking at the documents that Mr. Milosevic had signed. If somebody claims that there is a document through which he overstepped his authority, then I'd have to have this document shown to me. I'm not the Prosecutor here, you see. I can provide expertise only on matters that are contentious and where people tell me, Yes, it seems to us that this document was adopted as authority was overstepped. I'm an expert in that. I can provide my expert opinion on that, but if you're asking me whether Mr. Milosevic or somebody else had the power or might to resolve things by simple glances, that is terra nostra to me. I have no knowledge about that. If you're asking me whether he had a Praetorian Guard or not, I cannot judge a man that way even in a restaurant or in the street let alone in this kind of a situation. I hope that you understand my position. As for -- well, we could talk now about what different authors in the field of constitutional law have written, but, you know, we scholars are used to looking at all this stuff until our eyes pop out, but we just have to see things in order to be able to discuss matters. Whoever speaks in the field of law a priori has missed his calling, I believe. Your Honour, Judge Bonomy, if I may address you. May I correct myself in respect of an answer I gave you to one of your questions in the first part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a teacher of young students, when I was conducting examinations, I was not really inclined to accept self-corrections, but ultimately I would accept them. In the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - I've been thinking about this during the break - there was a Federal Ministry of the Interior, but it was reduced only to international police cooperation or the appearance of the federal state in international police cooperation when only the federal state could act rather than the federal units and the like. I kindly ask you to take into account this self-correction of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Professor, what do you kindly understand -- how do you distinguish between constitution and constitutionalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now we are going into theoretical debates and differences in legal civilizations. The country that you come from, Your Honour - it's Pakistan, I believe - in part it is inclined towards Anglo-Saxon tradition due to historical circumstances. Then I can understand the distinction that you're making between a written constitution and a live constitution, as people say in my legal culture. After all, a great deal was written about that in the 1950s and the 1960s when constitutions were discussed, those that were alive and those that were not in part. However, regrettably that debate was coloured by ideological hues, regrettably. At that time, there was a free world and an enslaved world, so this debate could not yield full results. One knows how a constitution is defined in European continental theory and everywhere where it appears in a written form. On the other hand, one knows what constitutionality is in constitutionalism in countries that do not have a written constitution. In the country where I was born and where I lived until the age of 35, what prevailed was the tradition of written constitutions, and constitutional law was studied by studying the constitution and regulations dealing with the way in which the state and government function. Of course, there are human rights and freedoms, too, but that is something that is unavoidable. It is precisely for that reason that my analysis is the way it is, and it has to do with norms, legal sources, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things I've learned this morning is that you were a deputy foreign minister of the Republika Srpska during part of the period when Milosevic was the president of the federal republic. During the break, I'll consider the extent to which I wish to press you on matters beyond your expertise. Meanwhile, we'll continue with the cross-examination by Mr. Hannis, and if the issue arises again and has to be adjudicated on, then we'll take the break early to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, did you ever hear of a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija that existed in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I really have to admit that I have not heard of it. Also, an organ under that name is not mentioned in the relevant legal sources regulating the field of defence and the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your expertise and your study, there's nothing in the constitution that would provide for such a body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say to you that there is no such organ. There is no such organ in the constitution, in the Law on Defence, or in the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about a body called the operations inter-departmental staff for suppressing terrorism or combatting terrorism?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I really haven't heard of that body, and that body is not mentioned in the kind of legal sources that I was telling you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to coming to testify here, did you follow any of this trial or the Slobodan Milosevic trial by watching on TV or reading newspaper accounts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I really did not follow trials on television because for years I've been watching sports only on TV and a film or two. I read some things in the newspaper, but you know what it's like. Newspaper articles can be very sparse, and the journalists writing about these things usually only have a general education, at university level, of course. So one cannot rely on everything they write, let alone the precision in the use of words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that you were likely to come and testify as a witness at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's been a couple of years now. I think -- I think it's been two years now, a year and a half perhaps. I really haven't kept any records on this precisely because this was a difficult period in my life, you remember from the questions you put to me about that, so time seemed to fly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that approximate two years, you didn't have any curiosity about the proceedings or the personalities here? You never bothered to see what was happening in this trial, knowing that you were going to be a witness?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in the broadest possible terms, from the newspapers, if that's of any interest to you. I read Politika daily, regularly, but not all of it, but I have had no interest in that because I have other things that I do in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in dealing with your expert report about the federal cabinet and its relationship with other components of the government and the president of the republic, et cetera, did you have occasion to speak with anybody, such as Mr. Sainovic or Mr. Bulatovic, who had a role to play during 1998 and 1999? Did you talk to any of those people about their jobs or their experiences?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please specify. When do you mean? When was I supposed to have talked to them? 1998, 1999, 2002, while they were at large, while they were in Scheveningen? I'm asking you this. It's a bona fide question. I just want to -- want you to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right now I'm limiting my question to since the time you became aware that you might be called as a witness here and in preparing your expert report, did you speak to Nikola Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no. This might sound in bad taste, but I agreed with the Defence as to what the topic of my expert report would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Given the limited topic, I had no call to talk to Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You have answered my question. Was it the same answer for Mr. Bulatovic, who was the prime minister back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your -- well, let me ask you one more question before I get to that last one. You may not be aware, we have an exhibit in this case which is P2166. If we could put that up on the screen with the English and B/C/S side by side. I want to ask you a question related to the constitutional authority of the president vis-a-vis other personnel. Professor, this is a document that purports to be the minutes of a meeting on the 29th of October, 1998, at the Beli Dvor palace in Belgrade. It's described as a minutes of the meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo. The meeting was chaired by the president, Mr. Milosevic, and you'll see among those attending are the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic; we have the president of the chamber of citizens of the Federal Assembly, Mr. Minic; we have the deputy prime minister, Mr. Sainovic; we have the minister of interior for the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Stojiljkovic; we have General Perisic as the Chief of Staff; some other military guys; some other police generals. So we have the president of the republic of the FRY, the president of the Republic of Serbia, somebody -- the chairman or the president of the Chambers of Citizens from the Federal Assembly, a deputy prime minister, the minister of the interior for Serbia, these are people from both the federal government and the republic government, from the army and the police; this meeting is chaired by the president. Was there a constitutional provision allowing for Mr. Milosevic to create this kind of body and chair this kind of body? There wasn't, was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would make our work more efficient if the expert would be allowed to look at this document, not just a heading on page 1, but to look at it in its entirety and then perhaps to answer some questions in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never seen this document before, and I haven't seen any of the documents of this kind, indeed, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Hannis, what do you say to what Mr. Petrovic says?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy if we can make a copy and take a break now and let him come back and answer our question then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can do that. We need to have a break around this time, anyway. You'll be given a copy of the document to have a look at during the break, this time for half an hour, and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, did you have adequate time during the break to look at that exhibit, P2166?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Not enough time, but enough to get an impression -- well, I can't go any further than that in this context, but it should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you make any comment on what you can say based on this document regarding President Milosevic's role in interrelationship with the federal government and these other organs represented by the people attending this meeting on the 29th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: About the relationship of President Milosevic and the federal government and the people who were present there, I can't tell you anything about that, but I can tell you what my personal opinion is about what I've read with a lot of caveats because there is a lot of other material that is missing, and it would be as follows: So I'm not giving you an answer to the question about the relationship between President Milosevic and the federal government and the people, the officials of the state government who were present there because I don't know anything about that. The document that you gave me - and this is the first time that I see it - I tried to put it in the context of legal norms about the competence of state organs and in the context of legal norms about the documents -- or legal documents enacted by those state authorities. I was able to ascertain, and this is not difficult. If we look at the constitution, the Law on Defence, and the Law on the Army, since the Rules of Service in the Yugoslav Army were not consulted by me and I didn't have an opportunity to look at them before, I ascertained that I am missing the document establishing the operations inter-departmental staff if such a document exists. I was also able to ascertain that within the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, this organ, if it is an organ indeed - I cannot say that because I don't have the act on its establishment - if such a document exists, this group of people, this set of people, at page 16 in relation to everything that is said here - and let me tell you right in advance that I did not have an opportunity to read everything in detail - did not issue any acts or orders. Under our system, conclusions are not individual legal acts or separate legal acts or orders. This is uncontroversial. In our system, conclusions are made by some administrative organs in some secondary issues. In Article 4 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, it is stipulated - that's paragraph 2 - that the president of the republic in performing tasks from paragraph 2 of this article shall issue orders, commands, and decisions. The General Staff implementing the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to read a little bit slower when reading legal documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, could you speak a bit more slowly, please, when you're reading. There's a temptation for all of us to speak much too quickly, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, indeed. So the Chief of the General Staff in implementing the statutory documents or legal documents enacted by the president of the republic shall issue rules, orders, commands, instructions, and other legal acts. On the other hand, it is also stipulated in the Law on Defence - please bear with me as I'm trying to find my way in this heap of papers - it is stipulated that the Supreme Defence Council shall issue documents that shall be entitled the defence plan of the country, the decisions in accordance with which the president of the republic shall command the army, shall exercise command over the army, shall establish the strategy for armed struggle, and so on, so that you cannot really find any order or any legal document that would be called a conclusion. On the other hand, it is quite clear that in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as it was at the time, despite the fact that the federalist principle was in force, the federal organs had to eo ipso cooperate with the organs of the member republics, to cooperate with them. The member states had to cooperate with each other, and despite the fact that the government in the Republic of Yugoslavia was set up on the principle of the separation of powers, the organs of the federal state did not operate in isolation, but they also had to cooperate, to consult each other, and so on. On the basis of this document, the document that you've given me, I say it again, on the basis of this document and without having access to any other evidence that pertains to this document, I can only conclude on the basis of what we can read at page 16 and on the basis of the exchange of information that is done here relating to certain military and police actions, this is some kind of a consultative meeting of various people because I really don't have anything on which to base any other conclusion. Of course, I fully take into account the fact that it says here that this was issued by the military cabinet of the president of the republic, but this fact is not enough. Since I don't have a document establishing this body within the system of command or as a state organ of this particular body, either as a permanent body or as an ad hoc body, so I cannot reach any other conclusions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you reach a conclusion as to whether or not President Milosevic was acting within or beyond his constitutional powers in setting up such a body and chairing such a body?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that because I don't have the act on its --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if you allow me. The interpretation by my learned colleague Mr. Hannis I think does not correspond to the facts, especially the facts of this case, and in particular of -- with what this witness has in front of him. So we want him to establish a foundation for his claim as to why this body was set up, and then we can ask the witness to give us his answer about the merit of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the reference -- the main subjects of this meeting appears to be a report or reports about the work of a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no. Mention is made of the Joint Command, but apart from page 1 and in several other places, that's the only places where I found this Joint Command being mentioned. So I can't tell you anything about its functioning, its existence, because I don't have any legal document establishing that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But my question was: Would you agree with me that most of this document, most of the meeting, dealt with discussing the work of the Joint Command between July 25th and 29 October 1998? That's the bulk of what this document is about, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, most of this document, as far as I was able to see in the brief period of time, concerns the exchange of information between Lieutenant-General Nebojsa Pavkovic, the commander of the Pristina Corps, and -- well, I don't want to now enumerate all the officials, state officials that attended this meeting. The Joint Command is mentioned at one point here, and I actually didn't find it mentioned so many times to be able to say that this document deals with the Joint Command. I read the reports presented by all those officials about what was done in their -- within their purview. Well, you can go through -- but you have to bear in mind that you have had this document for years, and I only had 25 minutes to look at it. You have to bear that at mind. At page 7 there is mention of it, maybe three or four other places -- well, I can't tell you now whether this is really focused on the Joint Command. I read this as a series of reports by people who were all in charge of implementing certain military or police measures in Kosovo or perhaps as part of some other task that is not of a military or a police nature because, after all, there are people here who are not state officials at all. For instance, I was able to see that the deputy president of the Serbian Socialist Party, Dusan Matkovic, so I really can't say that I agree with you when you say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in fairness to you because you had such a short time, I won't press you on that. But do you find -- is there any provision in the constitution for a body such as a Joint Command based on what you're able to understand about what the Joint Command was from reading -- from your brief review of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears to me that this has been asked and answered in the first part of the cross-examination by my learned colleague Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It has actually, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While this document is before us, can you from your experience think of any other similar example of a body that existed in some form within the federal republic headed up by the president comprising representatives from the army -- senior representatives from the army and the police from the federal government and the republican government, that's the Republic of Serbia, and there was no order, decision, conclusion, or any other formal process or document establishing it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, based on what I know I did not have any encounter with such bodies, not in the literature, not through any documents, and least of all through any -- my personal contacts or personal knowledge. We have the concept of consultation, the consultation by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the president or the head of state, head of any other state. This is done when it is necessary to designate the prime minister-elect, the federal prime minister-elect. For instance, the president of the republic also presents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please confine yourself to my questions. If it's something you really think needs to be added to make sure the full picture is understood, then you should give that information, but I think you're going on to a different area now. I really would like to know whether you as a constitutional expert would expect that a body such as this would have been constituted in a formal way, there would be some formal document recording its establishment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: If such a body makes decisions, legal documents or acts of command, then yes; but if not, in every state, a head of -- the head of state can have this kind of consultations because how would he gain knowledge in light of the fact that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia represents the state in the country and abroad? I'm just giving you this as an example. So if it issues legally binding documents and acts of command, then there has to be a legal basis for its establishment; if not, then this is an acceptable form of -- forum for meeting, consultations, exchange of information, and so on, among those various organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, following on from that, is it the case that the president of the FRY had no formal relationship with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: He did not have powers over the Serbian MUP, but you have to bear in mind the fact that something that was -- that no federal police existed. There was no police at the federal level. You have to bear in mind that this was a federal state and that in part of its territory there was a disturbance of the peace, whichever term you want to use. And at that time, in a way, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia joined with one of its republic -- member republics in an effort to settle the situation. So this form of cooperation is permissible because the laws stipulate when units of the Ministry of the Interior - we're talking about laws on police - when they can participate in certain police actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you use the expression "... this form of cooperation is permissible ..." and in that context you're talking about the federal authorities cooperating with the Serbian MUP. What do you mean by "this form of cooperation"? Could you be more precise about that? What is the form of cooperation you see occurring from these minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: What form of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You have used the expression "... this form of cooperation is permissible ..." so you as an expert think that something in here is permissible, and I would like you to define what that form of cooperation is that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this gathering did not issue any kind of legal decision or document of command, of course it's permissible to cooperate by exchanging information concerning the situation in Kosovo in this case, but basically information about anything. How, otherwise, could the president of the state command the Army of Yugoslavia, for example? Everywhere in the world where there are federal units and federal officials, they meet; they exchange information so that each one can later on arrive at the appropriate legal decisions within his own sphere of competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in relation to the MUP of Serbia, what is it that you say you can draw from this -- these minutes about the cooperation that was occurring between the federal authorities and the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see here that General -- or rather, Major Sreten Lukic informed this gathering about the police actions which the police forces engaged there in Kosovo had gathered out. Exchange of information amounts to cooperation. Noncooperation is when there is no exchange of information and no mutual contact. So I'm referring to the form of cooperation that I see here, and this is exchange of information. Let me repeat, there's no command document or any other legal document that would enable me to draw any other legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if we're looking at the same part of this document when you say that, Major-General Sreten Lukic reported or submitted a report on the work of what's called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this is. What's it called: The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. I have no documents concerning all this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but that's the cooperation that's taking place. The cooperation, if it's Lukic you're thinking about, it's the cooperation between the Joint Command and the federal authorities, apparently. You see, that's why I want to understand what it is you mean by "this form of cooperation that is permissible."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking of cooperation from this, through exchange of information, based on this, because as for other forms of cooperation, strategic, tactical, and so on, I don't know anything about that. I'm not a military expert. I didn't get very far in the army. I was just a corporal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things that General Lukic reported to this meeting was about an agreement reached between President Milosevic and a US envoy called Holbrooke about the reduction in the number of MUP forces in Kosovo. What authority would Milosevic have to agree to a reduction in MUP forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the Constitution of the FRY, in international and internal relations it is represented by the president of the republic. In paragraph 1 of Article 96, it says that the president of the republic represents the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at home and abroad. On the other hand, I didn't look at this Law on Foreign Affairs here, but it's well known in international law that there are three organs which are authorised without any additional authorisation to sign international treaties, agreements, and so on. That's the head of state, the prime minister, and the minister of foreign affairs. As a lawyer, this is where I see the connection because it should not be forgotten that the FRY at that time was a unique and unified international legal subject, whereas its -- it was a single subject, in other words, and its member states were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a matter of some importance to us, and your opinion would assist us. You're saying that somehow or other the president of the FRY has authority to agree to a reduction in the numbers of MUP forces present in Kosovo, which is a part of the Republic of Serbia, just because he's talking about it to some foreign representative who wants to poke his nose in?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know many details, but I can recall that Mr. Holbrooke arrived here as a representative probably of the president or the State Department of the USA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, according to General Lukic he was a representative of the international community, even wider than that. But what I'm trying to understand from --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: All the more so, all the more so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But what I'm trying to understand is how does that give rise to a situation where President Milosevic can reach agreement about the reduction of MUP forces within Serbia? What is the constitutional provision that gives him that power?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as is stated in Article 1 of its constitution, is a sovereign federal state founded on the equality of citizens and the equality of its member republics. Just a moment. In Article 16 [as interpreted], it says that: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia shall fulfil in good faith" -- oh, yes. "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia shall fulfil in good faith the obligations contained in international treaties to which it is a contracting party."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: In Article 7, it says that: "A member republic within its competences may maintain relations with foreign states but not to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or any of its other member republics." In Article 77 of the constitution, it says -- just a moment, please, that: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia shall through its organs formulate policy, enact and enforce federal legislation, and ... in matters concerning," and then, 6, international relations. That's item 6. And Article 96, paragraph 1, which I have already quoted, all of this taken together can give the answer to the question as to who can conclude international treaties or agreements on behalf of Yugoslavia. It can be done by the president of the FRY, the prime minister, or the minister of foreign affairs. How this agreement was reached, I don't know, but I am trying to see whether it can be brought into line with constitutional norms. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can return to this tomorrow because your evidence will continue tomorrow, and you can think about that and possibly expand upon your answer then, and I will turn to something else. One of the articles you referred to in the constitution today was Article 77, and you referred in particular to two parts of it, part 6 and 7. Can I ask you a little more about 6, which says that the -- and you've just referred to it again a moment ago, the general part. But it goes further than that. It talks, also, of "border crossing and control of the circulation of goods, services, and passengers across the border, the status of aliens and foreign artificial persons." Now, the evidence in this case suggests that all of these functions were carried out by the republican MUP. Can you explain how that fits into the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course. It is usual to have a constitutional law alongside the constitution regulating issues which are sometimes complex dealing with the transition from one constitutional regimen to another which is partially changed. With respect to your question, a constitutional law was passed, and the enactment of that law is envisaged in Article 143 of the Constitution of the FRY, and a dead-line is set for its enactment, and this law was amended more than once because the FRY, as we say, based on certain material, sources of legal norms, was not in a position to undertake it so that the dead-line was constantly pushed back by the constitutional law, and that's why there was a delay in regulating these issues, and unfortunately the state lasted -- did not last for long enough for us to see how it would have been regulated in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I fully understand that. I understand that there may be difficulties in transition, but is there some provision of a constitutional nature that says that these jobs should meanwhile be done by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's understood. It goes without saying. Because the time-limit, the dead-line by which the laws regulating these issues kept being pushed back in a legally permitted manner, that is, the constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Where it says which laws shall cease to be in force, when, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that the SFRY did not control the borders?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, control of the borders, that's a detail I did not deal with here, but I know that there was dual control of the border at the time. It was controlled partly by the army and partly by the police in various areas, and that's as far as my knowledge of this matter goes. Recently, the system of control of the border was changed, and civil control of border crossings and of the border in general is now implemented, as is usual in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if there's a provision in the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia dealing with their role in controlling the border?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: With the best will in the world, at this point in time I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we also can return to that one tomorrow. You've indicated that you worked in the Institute of Comparative Law Studies in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: During what period?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: In the period from November 2003 -- no, 2003 -- 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to April 2000. First I worked full time, and as of November, one-third of work time, part time, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was your specialist subject then?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: We worked on several projects at the time funded by the federal government, and each one of us had to write a certain number of papers in the area of comparative law, either comparing legal institutes or describing certain legal institutes in the world or in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, to what extent, then, were you dealing with issues of constitutional law or issues that can be said to relate to constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, I dealt mainly with issues concerning constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, the new constitutional order of Russia, of the Baltic states, the position of the government in the UK or Great Britain and Northern Ireland and so on. Those were the issues I dealt with at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And my understanding is that this is an institute with a high reputation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I would be glad to have worked in such an institute. Yes, at that time it was held in high esteem, especially when it was headed by a professor, Professor Slobodan Blagojevic. That was up to the 1980s. At that time, it was held in very high esteem. He was a professor of the faculty of law in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your period there was 1993 to 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how much of your time, then, was spent living in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Two days. On Mondays and Thursdays, that's when I was at work in the institute, and the rest -- for the rest of the time we worked where we could because at that time there was a shortage of space in the institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if my question was perhaps fully interpreted to you. I'm anxious to know how much of your time you lived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Two days a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you travelled back to Bosnia twice a week?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in your comparative constitutional law studies or any other constitutional law studies, have you ever come across a book or an article suggesting that President Milosevic acted beyond his legal powers, in either Serbia when he was president there or Yugoslavia when he was president there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Not in the constitutional legal scholarly literature, but I didn't read many articles of that type because my professional curiosity went in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you had a role in the Dayton peace negotiations. What exactly was your role there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time of my participation in all peace negotiations from 1991 onwards, I was a member of a delegation going to Dayton dealing with legal and constitutional issues. I was there as a legal expert. I took my Ph.D. at the chair of constitutional law at the faculty in Belgrade, and my Ph.D. thesis had to do with the constitutional order of the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you involved in -- at the end of the day when these negotiations achieved a result?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Dayton all the time, until the agreement was initialled, until the very last day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was Milosevic involved in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic was in Dayton also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was his role in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of some preliminary agreements. He was the president -- or rather, the head of the joint delegation of Serbia and Republika Srpska, if I recall correctly, and this happened after numerous negotiations between the -- with the representatives of the contact group and especially the USA, just as the agreement concerning Northern Ireland was reached through the activity of the USA and the secessionist side lost and the other side and advocating different solutions achieved its goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was it within the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia at that time that gave him the power to head a joint delegation in negotiations such as this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It was an agreement achieved under the auspices of Mr. Holbrooke in a situation which - how shall I put it -- cannot easily be made to fit a regular situation. There was pressure from the members of the contact group, and this was an agreement between the organs of Republika Srpska and the organs of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a number of matters still to deal with, and there may be questions also from Mr. Petrovic when I am finished, so you will require to return tomorrow to continue and complete your evidence. That will be -- yeah, that's at 9.00 tomorrow in this court. So all I need to say to you at the moment is be back here at 9.00 tomorrow. I have another administrative matter to deal with, so if you could please leave the courtroom. We'll see you at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's unlikely that the evidence of Professor Lukic will take a great deal of time tomorrow. The next witness will be a Chamber witness, General Djakovic, but there will be one or two other issues to be addressed when we get to the end of the professor's evidence. It seems to us that the best plan is to postpone the evidence of General Djakovic until Monday and to deal with anything that's outstanding tomorrow. I hope that that does not inconvenience anyone, but although time was booked to sit until 3.30 tomorrow, it's not very likely that we will occupy any part of the afternoon session, and, indeed, we'll probably be finished fairly quickly. Mr. Fila, you've raised informally an issue over the order of the examination of Chamber witnesses, and we can address that at some time tomorrow. We'll -- and if there are any other administrative issues that parties are concerned about, they can be raised tomorrow and - just a second - counsel for each accused should be in a position to state clearly what, if anything, remains outstanding in respect of the presentation of their cases. So we can adjourn now, can we, Mr. Fila, until 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of May, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
